title: Electromagnetic Spectrum Infographic
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: AP Chemistry
description: Interactive electromagnetic spectrum on a logarithmic scale with aligned wavelength, frequency, and photon energy rulers and a magnified view of visible light. A movable marker shows the region, how it interacts with matter, and the frequency and photon energy calculated from c = wavelength x frequency and E = hf.

learningObjectives: Identify the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order
Compare the relative wavelength, frequency, and photon energy of different types of radiation using c = wavelength x frequency and E = hf
standards: AP Chemistry CED Unit 3: Intermolecular Forces and Properties (spectroscopy and the electromagnetic spectrum, photoelectric effect)

controls.label: Wavelength
controls.description: Logarithmic wavelength from 10^3 m to 10^-13 m; sliding right shortens the wavelength

controls.label: Example
controls.description: Jumps the marker to a real source such as an FM radio station, a microwave oven, or a medical X-ray

controls.label: Spectrum bar, rulers, and magnified visible strip
controls.description: Click or drag to place the marker

assumptions: Region boundaries follow common textbook conventions and are approximate
Visible light is taken as 400 nm to 700 nm, matching the chapter text

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Labeled diagram with a movable marker and concrete calculated values
keyQuestions: Which region has the longest wavelength? The highest photon energy?
Why does frequency increase when wavelength decreases?
Why can ultraviolet light break bonds when infrared light cannot?
commonMisconceptions: Visible light makes up a large part of the spectrum
Different regions travel at different speeds
assessmentOpportunities: Rank three sources by wavelength, frequency, and photon energy without the MicroSim, then check
